title: How chatbots like ChatGPT work
examples: How do these chatbots actually learn to talk?
If they are trained on the internet, do they know everything?
What makes them sound so human sometimes?

explain.say: Today we will learn how chatbots like ChatGPT actually work. These programs use very advanced computer science.

items: Input prompt: User asks a question
Model processes text: Converts words to numbers
Prediction: Calculates the most likely next word
Output: Presents the chosen word to the user

explain.say: The core idea is predicting the next word in a sentence. It does not truly understand meaning like people do.
Chatbots are trained on massive amounts of text data. This training helps them recognize patterns in language.
Because they see so much text, they learn grammar and common phrases. They build a statistical map of language.
A real-life example is writing an email. If you start with 'Dear Mr Smith, I am writing to...', the chatbot suggests the next logical phrase.
A common mistake is assuming the chatbot knows facts perfectly. It only predicts what sounds right, not what is true.

items: It can combine known patterns incorrectly.

faq.q: Do chatbots actually think for themselves?
faq.a: No, they do not think like humans do. They are complex pattern matching systems that predict the most probable sequence of words.

faq.q: If they are trained on the internet, do they know everything?
faq.a: No, their knowledge is limited by the data they were trained on. They can only repeat patterns found in that data.
asks: Are they up to date on everything?

faq.q: Why do they sometimes give wrong answers?
faq.a: They can generate text that sounds highly convincing but is factually incorrect. This is because predicting what sounds plausible is not the same as knowing the truth.
asks: How can I check if they are lying?

faq.q: What is the difference between prediction and understanding?
faq.a: Understanding requires grasping context and meaning, while prediction only requires knowing which word statistically follows another. The chatbot excels at the latter.
asks: Is predicting the same as knowing?
What is the difference between syntax and semantics?

faq.q: Can I ask them questions about things that happened yesterday?
faq.a: Their knowledge is based on their last training update. They might not know about very recent events unless they are connected to live search tools.

facts: Chatbots operate by calculating the probability of the next word.
Their training data is drawn from vast collections of human-generated text.
They are excellent at recognizing linguistic patterns but lack true comprehension.
The output is a statistical prediction, not a statement of verified fact.

quiz.say: If a chatbot reads 'The capital of France is...', what is the most likely next word?
quiz.why: The training data overwhelmingly links 'France' with 'Paris' as its capital.

wrong.1: London is the capital of England, not France.
wrong.2: This is an adjective, not the name of the city.

quiz.say: If a chatbot generates a sequence of words that sounds perfect but is factually wrong, what is this limitation called?
quiz.why: Hallucination describes the creation of convincing but false information.

wrong.0: Overfitting means the model memorized the training data too well.
wrong.1: Bias relates to favoring certain viewpoints in the data.
wrong.2: Lagging refers to outdated information, not the creation of false facts.

quiz.say: When a chatbot predicts the next word, what mathematical concept is it primarily using?
quiz.why: It calculates the likelihood or probability of one word following another.

wrong.0: Causality requires knowing cause and effect, which is beyond prediction.
wrong.1: Syntax only deals with sentence structure, not the likelihood of the whole sequence.
wrong.3: Logic implies understanding rules, which the chatbot does not possess.
